Differential for the progressive syndrome includes logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia (typically Alzheimer pathology), posterior cortical atrophy (also Alzheimer‑related), early‑onset Alzheimer disease with predominant posterior involvement, and an iatrogenic amyloid‑beta/tauopathy linked to the historic growth‑hormone treatment; a contribution from chronic vascular cognitive impairment secondary to the prior hemorrhage must also be considered. Next evidence needed to distinguish these causes: amyloid PET or CSF Aβ42/tau profile to assess Alzheimer‑type pathology; tau PET or CSF phosphorylated tau to differentiate typical AD from atypical variants; high‑resolution MRI volumetry for posterior cortical atrophy versus focal atrophy from the old hemorrhage; PRNP sequencing and RT‑QuIC if prion disease is suspected; and, if feasible, APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 genetic testing to exclude autosomal‑dominant AD. Additional supportive data would include comprehensive neuropsychological profiling to map language and visuospatial domains, FDG‑PET to identify posterior hypometabolism, and susceptibility‑weighted imaging to quantify cerebral microbleeds that may reflect amyloid angiopathy.
